name: Big Bone Lick
subtitle: Boone County / salt lick & fossil beds
history: Big Bone Lick was a mineral spring where Pleistocene mastodons, mammoths, and ground sloths left bones in the mud while seeking salt. Native peoples and later explorers—including Christopher Gist—collected fossils here; Thomas Jefferson later studied specimens from the lick. The site became Big Bone Lick State Historic Site, one of Kentucky’s earliest windows on deep time and a waypoint for salt hunters on the Ohio frontier.

name: Lexington Named
subtitle: Fayette County / McConnell Springs
history: In early June 1775, William McConnell’s surveyors camped on a sinking spring of Elkhorn Creek when word arrived of the April 19 fight at Lexington, Massachusetts. They named the camp for that battle and returned east; permanent settlement waited until 1779, when Robert Patterson’s party built a blockhouse near present Main and Mill. Virginia established the town in 1782—the springs chose the site, the Revolution chose the name.

name: Benjamin Logan / Logan's Station
subtitle: Lincoln County / St. Asaph near Stanford
history: In 1775 Benjamin Logan left Boone's party and built Logan's Station (St. Asaph) near present-day Stanford—a stockade by Buffalo Spring that held through a roughly thirteen-day siege in May 1777. Logan hauled the wounded Burr Harrison inside under fire, then slipped out at night and walked about 150 miles to the Holston settlements for powder. He later helped write Kentucky's first constitution and settled on Bullskin Creek near Finchville in Shelby County.

name: Shelbyville Founding
subtitle: Shelby County seat / Clear Creek
history: Shelby County was carved from Jefferson County in 1792 and named for first governor Isaac Shelby. That October, at the first county court, Revolutionary veteran William Shannon donated about 50 acres on Clear Creek so the new seat would sit on the Frankfort-to-Falls road. Trustees required hewed-log houses with brick or stone chimneys; by 1800 the town had 262 people. Nearby Squire Boone's Painted Stone Station had been the earlier foothold—Shelbyville won the courthouse.

name: Chickasaw / Jackson Purchase
subtitle: Western Kentucky / 1818 treaty
history: West of the Tennessee River, Chickasaw hunting grounds stayed off Kentucky's settled map until October 19, 1818. Andrew Jackson and Isaac Shelby negotiated what became the Jackson Purchase: roughly 13,000 square miles (about 2,369 in Kentucky) for annuities. That treaty filled in the western counties from Ballard through McCracken and closed the last big Indigenous title claim inside the state.

name: Frankfort Founding
subtitle: Franklin County / Frank's Ford capital
history: Before it was the capital, the site was a buffalo-trail ford on the Kentucky River. In 1780 pioneer Stephen Frank was killed in a skirmish there; settlers called the crossing Frank's Ford, which shortened to Frankfort. In 1786 Virginia chartered a town on land promoted by Gen. James Wilkinson. When Kentucky became a state in 1792, Frankfort outbid rivals for the capital, and Gideon Shryock's Greek Revival Old Capitol (1830) finally stuck after earlier buildings burned.

name: Bullitt's Lick
subtitle: Bullitt County / Kentucky's first industry
history: Salt was frontier white gold, and the only large commercial saltworks west of the Alleghenies during the Revolution sat about three miles west of present-day Shepherdsville. Capt. Thomas Bullitt surveyed the Salt River lick in 1773; production started in 1779 as workers boiled brine in rows of iron kettles. Pack trains and flatboats carried the salt across Kentucky, a fort went up in 1780, and a boomtown nicknamed Saltburg grew around the furnaces until cheaper salt arrived around 1830.

name: George Rogers Clark / Corn Island
subtitle: Jefferson County / Falls of the Ohio
history: Virginia surveyor-turned-militia leader George Rogers Clark staged at Corn Island in the Falls of the Ohio in 1778, then launched the Illinois Campaign that took Kaskaskia and Vincennes from the British. The settlement he left behind became Louisville, chartered in 1780 and named for France’s Louis XVI. Fort Nelson later rose on the mainland as his western headquarters.

name: Battle of Blue Licks
subtitle: Robertson County · Aug 19, 1782 · McGary’s charge
history: On August 19, 1782, about 182 Kentucky militia chasing Captain William Caldwell’s raiders walked into an ambush on a Licking River ridge in today’s Robertson County. Major Hugh McGary commanded the center under Col. John Todd; when Boone warned of an ambush at the Licking Ford, McGary rode across daring anyone who wasn’t a coward to follow. Roughly seventy Kentuckians fell in minutes, including Todd, Trigg, and Boone’s son Israel. It was the settlers’ bloodiest Revolutionary defeat in Kentucky, months after Yorktown.

name: Great Saltpetre Cave
subtitle: Rockcastle County / War of 1812 powder
history: South of Mount Vernon in Rockcastle County, Great Saltpetre Cave was mined hard for calcium nitrate during the War of 1812, when British blockades cut off imported saltpeter for gunpowder. Dozens of workers (many enslaved) leached cave earth in wooden vats and shipped crystals to powder mills until trade reopened after 1815. The Rockcastle Karst Conservancy keeps the preserve today.

name: Richard Henderson / Transylvania
subtitle: Henderson County / Transylvania Company
history: North Carolina judge Richard Henderson reorganized his investors as the Transylvania Company in early 1775, then bargained at Sycamore Shoals for roughly 20 million acres between the Kentucky, Cumberland, and Ohio rivers. Cherokee headmen signed in mid-March; warrior Dragging Canoe opposed the sale and warned the country would become dark and bloody. Virginia later voided the private purchase but compensated the company with Ohio River acreage that seeded Henderson County.

name: Bardstown Founding
subtitle: Nelson County seat / Beech Fork
history: The Bardstown area was explored in the mid-1770s and briefly called Salem. In 1780 William Bard surveyed a town on a 1,000-acre grant for his brother David and John Cockey Owings and set aside ground for public buildings. Named seat of new Nelson County in 1784, it was chartered by Virginia as Baird’s Town in 1788 and settled into the name Bardstown—one of Kentucky’s oldest inland towns.

name: John Floyd / Floyd's Station
subtitle: Jefferson County / Beargrass Creek
history: Virginia surveyor John Floyd led a 1774 Fincastle party into Kentucky, staked 2,000 acres on Beargrass Creek, and came back in 1779 to stockade Floyd's Station near today's St. Matthews. Virginia made him a Louisville trustee, Jefferson militia colonel, and in 1783 one of Kentucky's first two judges. On April 8 that year he rode toward Bullitt's Lick in a scarlet coat; a shot from ambush dropped him, and he died two days later at 32.

name: Georgetown / Royal Spring
subtitle: Scott County / Elijah Craig spring
history: In July 1774 John Floyd claimed a thousand acres around a big Bluegrass spring. John McClelland built a cabin and stockade above it in 1775; an attack on December 29, 1776, killed McClelland, and the station emptied in 1777. Baptist preacher Elijah Craig later laid out Lebanon on the same spring, won a 1784 Virginia charter, and in 1790 renamed the place George Town for Washington. Scott County's seat still drinks from Royal Spring.

name: Leestown
subtitle: Franklin County / Kentucky River port
history: In 1773 the McAfee company and Hancock Taylor surveyed a buffalo crossing on the Kentucky River about a mile north of today’s Frankfort. Hancock and Willis Lee planted a village on the north bank in 1775, the first Anglo-American settlement north of the river. Raids emptied it in 1777; it returned as a tobacco warehouse and shipping port for hemp, corn, and whiskey, and in 1827 limestone for the Old State House was quarried from the riverbank here.

name: Squire Boone / Painted Stone / Long Run
subtitle: Shelby & Jefferson counties / 1781 massacre
history: Daniel's younger brother Squire Boone carved his name into a Clear Creek rock, painted the letters red, and by spring 1780 planted Shelby County's first large station about two miles north of present Shelbyville. After an April 1781 wound left Squire's right arm permanently short, most settlers fled toward Linn's Station and walked into the Long Run Massacre of September 13. He later rebuilt a mill on the burnt site before land debts cost him the station.

name: Paris Founding
subtitle: Bourbon County seat / 1789–1790
history: Joseph Houston's 1776 station sat near Doyle Spring. Lawrence Protzman later platted 250 acres and in 1789 got Virginia to charter the town as Hopewell as Bourbon County's seat. In 1790 James Garrard and locals renamed it Paris to match the county, itself named for France's Bourbon kings who backed the Revolution. The post office briefly ran as Bourbonton before Paris stuck.

name: Capt. Will Emery / Long Hunters
subtitle: Warren County / hunting-ground conflict
history: Shawnee held the larger northern and central Kentucky hunting grounds; Cherokee worked closer to Cumberland Gap. When long hunters stacked pelts for eastern markets, Native parties treated them as poachers. Around late 1769 a Shawnee band with Captain Will Emery took Boone and John Stewart’s six-month haul and warned them home: stay out, or the wasps and yellowjackets would sting. Not blank wilderness—a contested commons.

name: Christopher Gist / Ohio Company
subtitle: Fayette County / 1750–51 survey
history: Fifteen-plus years before Boone’s fame, the Ohio Company hired surveyor Christopher Gist to probe the Ohio Valley down toward the Falls. Crossing into Kentucky from the Scioto mouth, his journal logged rich bottomlands, canebrakes, buffalo plains, and Native towns. Shawnee at Lower Shawneetown warned him off the Falls; he brought the company a fossil “beest” tooth from Big Bone country and the first detailed English read of northeastern Kentucky.

name: Jacob Spears
subtitle: Bourbon County / early bourbon whiskey
history: Pennsylvania-born Revolutionary veteran Jacob Spears settled near Paris in Bourbon County and was distilling by the 1790s. Thomas Metcalfe built his stone house (“Stone Castle”) around 1790; the farm still holds a springhouse and whiskey storehouse—Kentucky’s most complete early distiller’s complex. Spears floated barrels down the Licking to the Ohio and on to New Orleans, and he is often credited among the first to market the county’s whiskey under the name that stuck: bourbon.

name: John Filson
subtitle: Jefferson County / Filson Club pin
history: Pennsylvania schoolteacher and surveyor John Filson reached Lexington around 1783 with land warrants for more than 12,000 acres. In 1784 he published The Discovery, Settlement and Present State of Kentucke—the first written history of the country—with a companion map engraved in Philadelphia. The book’s appendix carried the earliest printed Boone narrative; in 1788 Filson helped plat Losantiville (later Cincinnati) and that October vanished while surveying near the Great Miami.

name: Lexington & Ohio Railroad
subtitle: Franklin County / first KY railroad
history: On January 27, 1830, Kentucky chartered the Lexington & Ohio—the commonwealth’s first railroad, and among the first west of the Alleghenies—to tie Lexington to the Ohio River. Track used English strap iron spiked to quarried limestone sills; horses pulled early cars, then steam. The “Daniel Boone” engine made Lexington to Frankfort in about two and a half hours in 1835, cracking open Bluegrass freight toward the river long before the Civil War.

name: Bland W. Ballard / Tyler Station
subtitle: Shelby County / Tick Creek
history: Born Spotsylvania County, Va., October 16, 1761, Bland Williams Ballard came to Kentucky in 1779 and scouted for George Rogers Clark. With Robert Tyler he helped plant Tyler Station on Tick Creek east of Shelbyville around 1781. In 1788 Delaware warriors killed his father and several siblings near the station; Ballard fought through Fallen Timbers, survived capture at Frenchtown, represented Shelby County in the General Assembly, and died September 5, 1853. Ballard County carries his name.

name: Gaitskill Mound
subtitle: Montgomery County / Adena tablets
history: On Mount Sterling’s northern bypass, Gaitskill Mound is an Adena earthwork (roughly 800 B.C.–A.D. 700) listed on the National Register in 1975. Unlike many looted mounds, it yielded rare engraved stone and clay tablets recovered through University of Kentucky work associated with W.S. Webb—ritual objects tied to Adena cremation and mound ceremony rather than everyday trash. The site anchors Montgomery County’s deep Woodland past beneath the later townscape.

name: James C. Crow / Oscar Pepper
subtitle: Woodford County / Labrot & Graham ground
history: Scottish physician-chemist James C. Crow began advising Oscar Pepper's Woodford County farm still on Glenn's Creek by 1833. After Pepper rebuilt in stone (1837–38), Crow returned as master distiller (1840–55), measuring mash temperatures, yeast, and acidity with scientific care that fixed sour-mash practice as commercial habit. His whiskey shipped far beyond Kentucky; Old Crow later took his name, and the limestone valley still hosts Woodford Reserve on the old Pepper ground.

name: Isaac Shelby
subtitle: Lincoln County / Traveler's Rest
history: Maryland-born Isaac Shelby fought at Point Pleasant, then helped lead the Overmountain Men to victory at Kings Mountain in 1780. He moved to Kentucky in the 1780s, helped push statehood, and in 1792 became the commonwealth's first governor; sixteen years later he returned as fifth governor and led militia at the Battle of the Thames. Shelby County still carries his name, and Traveler's Rest marks his home ground.

name: William Whitley / Sportsman's Hill
subtitle: Lincoln County / Crab Orchard
history: Near Crab Orchard, William Whitley finished Sportsman's Hill (1787–1794), often called Kentucky's first brick house—thick walls, elevated windows, and hiding places against raids. Beside it he ran a clay oval where horses raced counter-clockwise, a pointed break from English turf clockwise. The house and hill remain a Lincoln County historic site.

name: Estill's Defeat
subtitle: Montgomery County / Little Mountain 1782
history: On March 22, 1782, Capt. James Estill and about 25 Lincoln County militiamen overtook a Wyandot raiding party at Little Mountain Creek, near today’s Mount Sterling. After nearly two hours of fighting, Lt. William Miller’s left flank broke, the Wyandots closed, and Estill was killed in hand-to-hand combat along with six of his men. The fight—also called the Battle of Little Mountain—was one of the bloodiest single engagements of Kentucky’s “Year of Blood.”

name: Cumberland Gap / Thomas Walker
subtitle: Bell County / geologic doorway
history: In March 1750 Dr. Thomas Walker led a Loyal Land Company party through the Appalachians and on April 13 recorded Cave Gap: a plain Indian road, a spring pouring from a cave, marked trees, and a pass visible for miles. He named the gap and nearby river for the Duke of Cumberland and later had a small cabin raised near present Barbourville—the first Euro-American house claimed in Kentucky. Walker’s journal mapped the geologic doorway later generations would pour through.

name: Catherine Spears Carpenter
subtitle: Casey County / 1818 sour-mash recipes
history: Twice-widowed Catherine Spears Carpenter ran a large Casey County farm after 1806, raising crops, livestock, and surplus corn into whiskey. County tax records show her paying on 100 gallons of spirits in 1815. An 1818 manuscript in the Carpenter Family Papers preserves sweet-mash and sour-mash distilling recipes she used to instruct her household—one of the earliest written American sour-mash records, decades before James Crow’s fame.

name: Wickliffe Mounds
subtitle: Ballard County / Mississippian town
history: Mississippian farmers founded Wickliffe around AD 1100 on a bluff over the Ohio, three miles from the Mississippi confluence. They built platform mounds, a plaza, houses, and after 1175 a cemetery mound; by 1350 the community capped its mounds and left. In the 1930s a promoter opened graves to tourists as “Ancient Buried City”; Murray State later professionalized the research, and the site became a state historic site in 2004.

name: Falls of the Ohio
subtitle: Clarksville / Jefferson fossil beds
history: About 390 million years ago a shallow Devonian sea laid down the Jeffersonville Limestone—coral banks and stromatoporoid sponges now exposed at the Falls of the Ohio. Those hard shelves made the only major rapids on the river, so flatboats had to portage; Louisville and the Indiana towns grew at that choke point. George Rogers Clark staged from Corn Island in 1778. The beds have been a National Natural Landmark since 1966.

name: Lower Shawneetown
subtitle: Greenup County / Scioto mouth KY bank
history: Long before stations dotted the Bluegrass, a major Shawnee town straddled the Ohio at the Scioto’s mouth near today’s South Portsmouth. English maps called it Lower Shawneetown; by 1751 eyewitnesses put the population around 1,200. It was a diplomatic hub and western end of Pennsylvania’s southern deerskin trade until 1758, when the Shawnee moved north. Kentucky archaeology still holds Fort Ancient pottery mixed with mid-1700s trade goods from the Bentley and related sites on the Kentucky bank.

name: Indian Knoll
subtitle: Late Archaic shell midden · Ohio County
history: Five thousand years before the first stations, Late Archaic hunter-gatherers kept returning to a shell midden on the Green River in Ohio County. Indian Knoll (15OH2) yielded over a thousand burials, twenty-three dog burials, and more than 50,000 artifacts when University of Kentucky crews dug it in the late 1930s WPA years. In the early 1990s it and nineteen other Green River shell middens became National Historic Landmarks.

name: Danville Constitution Square
subtitle: Boyle County / statehood conventions
history: After the Kentucky District court moved from Harrodsburg to Crow’s Station, Danville’s public square (laid out 1785) hosted ten conventions from 1784 to 1792. Delegates there framed the first state constitution in April 1792, clearing the way for Kentucky to enter the Union as the fifteenth state on June 1. Replicas of the log courthouse, jail, and meetinghouse still mark the ground.

name: Mount Horeb Adena / Adena Park
subtitle: Fayette County / UK Adena Park
history: Above Elkhorn Creek near Lexington, Adena people built a circular ditch-and-embankment enclosure more than 2,000 years ago for periodic ritual gatherings. WPA digs under William S. Webb in 1939 found a ring of large paired posts that likely screened ceremonies before the earthen walls went up. The University of Kentucky now protects a partially reconstructed site as Adena Park.

name: Fox Farm Fort Ancient
subtitle: Mason County / 15Ms1
history: On a broad ridgetop near Mays Lick, Fort Ancient farmers lived at Fox Farm (15Ms1) from about 1300 into the mid-1600s—one of the longest-lived villages of its kind in the Ohio Valley. Houses first ringed a plaza, then clustered around a large public building as population grew. Residents planted corn, beans, and squash, managed turkey harvests, and once curated eleven deer jaws as a ritual offering inside a house wall.

name: Indian Fort Mountain
subtitle: Madison County / Berea Pinnacles
history: On a knobby ridge south of Berea, dry-laid stone walls ring Indian Fort Mountain (15Ma25) in the Berea College Forest. Hopewell-era Middle Woodland people built them about 2,000 years ago as a hilltop enclosure, more a ceremonial marker than a stockade. Tests in 1980 treated the tumbled rock as linear mounds rather than a fighting wall. The site went on the National Register in 1983; hikers still climb the Pinnacles over the same ground.

name: Ashland Central Park Adena Mounds
subtitle: Boyd County / Central Park
history: Six conical Adena burial mounds still sit in Ashland’s Central Park, roughly 15–20 feet across and 4–6 feet high in a slight curve. UK archaeologists Webb and Funkhouser recorded them in 1932; a 1930s survey said no Kentucky city held more prehistoric evidence than Ashland, though many other local mounds were leveled for streets. Listed on the National Register in 1974, they mark Woodland mound-builder presence along the Ohio centuries before historic tribes.

name: Mount Sterling Founding
subtitle: Montgomery County seat / Little Mountain
history: Explorers out of Boonesborough called a tree-covered Adena burial mound “the Little Mountain.” Scotsman Hugh Forbes began selling lots beside it around 1790; in 1792 the Kentucky Assembly chartered the town on 640 acres. Forbes meant Mount Stirling (for Stirling, Scotland, plus the mound); the misspelled “Sterling” stuck. The mound—once about 25 feet high at Queen and Locust—was leveled in 1845, and Mount Sterling became Montgomery County’s seat.

name: Carlston Annis Shell Mound
subtitle: Butler County / 15Bt5
history: On the Green River floodplain in Butler County, Carlston Annis (15Bt5) is a Late Archaic shell midden about 300 by 350 feet and more than six feet thick, piled up beside a mussel shoal between roughly 3000 and 1000 BC. WPA crews under William S. Webb dug nearly half an acre in 1940–41; later work by the Shell Mound Archaeological Project refined the picture of repeated seasonal camps with burials, dog burials, hearths, and pestle caches.

name: Winchester Founding
subtitle: Clark County seat
history: Clark County was carved from Fayette and Bourbon on December 6, 1792, and named for George Rogers Clark. Justices first met at John Strode’s station, then voted to put the public buildings on John Baker’s land by his spring. On December 17, 1793, the Assembly established a town there named Winchester, after Baker’s hometown in Frederick County, Virginia. A two-room log courthouse went up in 1794; Winchester remains Clark’s seat.

name: Hardin Village Fort Ancient
subtitle: Greenup County / 15Gp22
history: On the Ohio floodplain in Greenup County near South Shore, Hardin Village was a late Fort Ancient town occupied from the late 1500s into the early 1600s and covering more than ten acres. University of Kentucky digs in 1939 and again in the 2010s mapped large bark-walled houses, storage pits, and family cemeteries. Triangular endscrapers point to intensive hide work for long-distance exchange—marine shell and brass among the imports—just as the protohistoric Ohio Valley was tipping toward abandonment.

name: Richmond Founding
subtitle: Madison County / Miller's barn courthouse
history: Madison County's first seat sat at hillside Milford with thin water. In 1798 the legislature let the court move onto Revolutionary War veteran Col. John Miller's land along Otter Creek; the county paid angry Milford residents before carting records to Miller's barn. On July 4, 1798, trustees named the new seat Richmond for Miller's Virginia birthplace, surveyed fifty acres into lots, and built a brick courthouse on the barn site in 1799. Richmond incorporated in 1809.

history: Basil Hayden Sr. led Maryland Catholic settlers to Pottinger's Creek in 1785; high-rye whiskey tradition and Holy Cross Church land mark early Nelson County bourbon and Catholic frontier settlement.

The mounds date to the Adena period (roughly 800 B.C.–A.D. 200), not the excavation year.

Chief Blackfish defended the town and was shot in the leg; he later died of the wound. The site lies north of the Ohio, outside Kentucky.

name: Cleek-McCabe Fort Ancient Village
subtitle: Boone County · circular village · occupation ~1200–1300 CE
history: On the Mud Lick Creek floodplain near Walton, Cleek-McCabe is a thirteenth-century Fort Ancient village: a ~100-foot-wide midden ring around a ~200-foot plaza, with low burial mounds east and west. UK crews in the late 1930s sampled the ring and dug the western mound; the eastern mound still stands. Under that western mound they found three successive roofless public buildings—first a 43-foot circle, then rectangles up to about 56 by 95 feet—sharing a central pole pit that links Fort Ancient ritual architecture to earlier Adena and Hopewell submound screens. Cordmarked jars with guilloche necks and triangular strap handles tie the pottery to Boone County and neighboring Ohio–Indiana Fort Ancient communities.

name: Jacob Beam / Hardin's Creek
subtitle: First barrel sale 1795 · Washington County (then)
history: In 1795 Jacob Beam (born Johannes Jacob Boehm) sold his first barrel of "Old Jake Beam" sour-mash whiskey from a corn farm and mill on Hardin's Creek in what was then Washington County, Kentucky. The family later grew the Old Tub brand; after Prohibition Jim Beam reopened the line, and seven generations still distill from that pioneer start.

name: Lancaster founding / Wallace’s Crossroads
subtitle: Garrard County seat · founded 1797 at Wallace’s Crossroads
history: Lancaster, the Garrard County seat, grew up around Revolutionary War Maj. Andrew Wallace’s settlement at Wallace’s Crossroads. Garrard County was formed in 1796 as Kentucky’s 25th county and named for Gov. James Garrard. In 1797 Capt. William Buford donated land for a town around the crossroads, and Joseph Bledsoe Jr. completed the survey and plat over the next year; the name came from Lancaster, Pennsylvania, either because a settler came from there or because the town followed a similar plan. Buford’s son Thomas was among the first town trustees in 1797. The post office opened in 1801 as “Lancaster Court House” (the name it kept until 1811), and the state assembly formally incorporated the city in 1837.

name: Peter Village enclosure (15Fa166)
subtitle: Fayette County · Early Woodland ditch-and-embankment · ~5th c. BCE
history: North of Lexington in Fayette County, Peter Village (15Fa166) is a huge Early Woodland ditch-and-embankment enclosure—about 9.2 hectares, irregular rather than a neat geometric circle. Long mislabeled an Adena “village,” it is better read as a specialized gathering and craft place; archaeologist Berle Clay tied it to barite and galena working, and newer geoarchaeology (Henry and others) points to dual embankments and construction as early as the 5th century BCE—among the earliest monumental enclosures in the Middle Ohio Valley. It sits near the better-known Mount Horeb circle, marking Bluegrass ritual landscapes centuries before forts and stations.

name: Read Shell Midden (15Bt10)
subtitle: Butler County · Late Archaic shell midden
history: On the Green River west of Morgantown, the Read Shell Midden (15Bt10) is a Late Archaic camp-and-cemetery in the same mussel-shoal world as Indian Knoll, Carlston Annis, and Ward. WPA crews dug it 1937–1939 under William S. Webb; more than 240 burials were identified. Occupation years are Late Archaic (~3000–1000 BC), not the dig dates. Approximate published coords (NRHP address restricted).

name: Stanford / St. Asaph (Logan’s Fort)
subtitle: Lincoln County · Standing Fort · county seat 1786
history: In spring 1775 Benjamin Logan and John Floyd’s survey party camped at Buffalo Spring and planted St. Asaph; Logan’s Fort rose there by early 1777 and never fell—nicknamed Standing Fort after the May 1777 siege. On May 16, 1786, the court seated permanently on Logan’s fifty-acre gift a mile east as Stanford, still Lincoln County’s seat.

name: Newt Kash Hollow (15Mf1)
subtitle: Menifee County · Early Woodland rockshelter
history: In Menifee County’s Red River country, Newt Kash rockshelter preserved Early Woodland plant beds—squash, sunflower, goosefoot, and sumpweed among the earliest clear domesticates from a Kentucky shelter, occupied intensively around 3,000 years ago. Later readings also treat the fiber, cradleboard, and medicinal plants as a possible women’s retreat and medicine place.

name: Col. John Todd of Lexington
subtitle: Fayette militia colonel · Blue Licks 1782 · Todd County
history: Pennsylvania-born lawyer John Todd (1750–1782) reached Kentucky around 1775, sat in Virginia’s legislature for Kentucky County, rode with George Rogers Clark to Kaskaskia and Vincennes, and was named civil commandant of Illinois County. He became Fayette’s first militia colonel and a Lexington trustee. After Bryan Station’s siege he led the pursuit that ended at Blue Licks on August 19, 1782, where he was killed at 32; Todd County (1819) still carries his name.

name: Muir Site (15Js86)
subtitle: Jessamine County · Early Fort Ancient Osborne Phase ~1010–1255 CE
history: Before the Nicholasville Bypass went in, University of Kentucky archaeologists dug the Muir site (15Js86) on a broad upland ridge west of Nicholasville. Radiocarbon and ceramics place it in the early Fort Ancient Osborne Phase, roughly 1010–1255 CE. Unlike later crowded plaza villages, Muir held only one to three rectangular single-set-post houses at a time, each with a shallow floor basin and central hearth—more a dispersed farmstead cluster than a stockaded town. Residents ate mostly deer, elk, and bear, grew corn, beans, knotweed, and sunflower, and made limestone-tempered jars with rare guilloche designs.
geocode_note: Wikipedia approximate location west of Nicholasville / Jessamine Creek ridge (site address not published).

photo.title: Main Street, Nicholasville

name: Newport at the Licking Mouth
subtitle: Campbell County · charter 1795 · Newport Barracks 1803
history: Hubbard Taylor platted the Ohio–Licking point for the family; James Taylor Jr. settled in 1793, pushed Campbell County through in 1794, and on December 14, 1795 the General Assembly chartered Newport on Taylor land. He named it for Admiral Christopher Newport of Jamestown fame, reserved a public square and riverfront common, and in 1803 sold the army five acres at the Licking mouth for what became Newport Barracks.

name: Adams Site (15Fu4)
subtitle: Fulton County · Mississippian town on Bayou de Chien
history: Near Hickman in Fulton County, on Bayou de Chien toward the Mississippi, the Adams Site is a Mississippian town built over an earlier Late Woodland village. Platform mounds around a central plaza (plus a smaller plaza southwest), deep village middens, and occupation roughly 1100–1500 CE place it with sister border towns like Wickliffe and Sassafras Ridge.

name: Drennon Springs
subtitle: Henry County · salt lick & early boiling works
history: In Henry County, Jacob Drennon and Matthew Bracken claimed the big salt lick on July 26, 1773; Nicholas Cresswell in 1775 described some fifty acres of buffalo-trampled ground and springs strong enough to leave salt crusts in the sun. Virginia’s Patrick Henry patented 400 acres including the springs to George Rogers Clark in 1785, and boiling works rose that winter.

name: Maj. Joseph Bowman
subtitle: Clark’s second-in-command · Harrodsburg petition 1776 · died 1779
history: Virginia-born Joseph Bowman came to Kentucky by 1775, signed the 1776 Harrodsburg county petition, and in 1778 raised a company for George Rogers Clark. As Clark’s second-in-command he took Prairie du Rocher, St. Philippe, and Cahokia after Kaskaskia fell, kept a day-by-day journal of the flooded winter march to Vincennes, and was promoted major just as a celebratory powder explosion burned him badly. He died at Fort Patrick Henry on about August 14–15, 1779 — the only American officer lost in the Illinois campaign.

name: Owensboro / Yellow Banks
subtitle: Smeathers cabin 1797 · town 1816–1817
history: Frontiersman William Smeathers (Bill Smothers) built a cabin on the south bank of the Ohio in 1797 at a landing flatboat men already called Yellow Banks for its clay bluffs. Daviess County was created in 1815; the town was laid out in 1816 and incorporated in 1817 as Owensborough for Col. Abraham Owen, killed at Tippecanoe in 1811 (the spelling shortened later). Smothers later scouted for Stephen F. Austin's Old Three Hundred in Texas. Downtown Smothers Park marks the home site — western Kentucky's river gate still sitting on that yellow bank.

photo.title: Second Street, Owensboro

name: Col. William Russell III
subtitle: Kings Mountain · Fayette 1783 · Russell County namesake
history: Born Culpeper County, Virginia, 1758; rode west on his father’s 1773 Kentucky attempt. Aide to Col. William Campbell at Kings Mountain; settled Fayette County in 1783 on military land. Early Kentucky house member, Northwest Indian War militia leader, and colonel of the 7th U.S. Infantry (Fort Harrison, Peoria War). Russell County is named for him.

name: Annis Mound & Village (15Bt2)
subtitle: Butler County · Middle Mississippian mound center
history: On the Green River’s Big Bend in Butler County, Annis (15Bt2 / 15Bt20) was a Middle Mississippian mound center occupied about 800–1300 CE, with expanding palisades and a large platform mound. Pinned from the 2026-09-17 KY History update (occupation years, not WPA/NRHP dates).

name: Cumberland Falls
subtitle: Rockcastle conglomerate · moonbow · gorge retreat
history: Where the Cumberland crosses hard Rockcastle conglomerate, softer rock below keeps a ~68-foot drop—the “Niagara of the South.” The falls retreated about 45 miles upstream cutting the gorge; clear full-moon nights bring a moonbow. Geology-focused pin (no modern park year).

name: Glasgow / Barren County seat
subtitle: John Gorin’s Big Spring · barrens · 1799
history: Barren County was authorized December 20, 1798, from Green and Warren, named for the open barrens prairie. In 1799 settlers chose John Gorin’s Big Spring for the county seat; Gorin opened a tavern that year and put land and cash toward public buildings on the pea-vine hill that became Glasgow’s square. The legislature recognized the town in 1809.

name: Maj. Silas Harlan / Harlan’s Station
subtitle: Salt River south of Harrodsburg · Blue Licks 1782
history: Virginia-born Major Silas Harlan (c. 1752–1782) came to Kentucky in 1774, built Harlan’s Station on the Salt River about seven miles south of Harrodsburg in 1778, and commanded spies in George Rogers Clark’s Illinois campaign. He fell leading an advance party at Blue Licks on August 19, 1782; Harlan County (1819) carries his name.

name: Chiggerville (15Oh1)
subtitle: Ohio County · Late Archaic Green River shell midden
history: On the Green River floodplain in Ohio County, the Late Archaic Chiggerville shell midden (roughly 3000–1000 BC) sits beside an old mussel shoal more than four feet thick. Digs recovered dense burials, hearths, mussels, fish, nuts, and Green River humped bannerstones—another node in Kentucky’s densest Archaic shell-midden landscape.

name: Salts Cave (15Ht4)
subtitle: Mammoth Cave NP · Early Woodland sulfate mining
history: Inside Mammoth Cave National Park, Salts Cave was one of several passages Early Woodland people used most intensively about 1000–200 BC. They mined wall sulfates—gypsum for pigment, mirabilite as medicine and seasoning—and carried cane torches, textile slippers, baskets, and gourd containers deep underground.

name: Capt. Jack Jouett / Craig’s Creek
subtitle: Midnight ride 1781 · in KY from 1782 · Woodford house 1797
history: On the night of June 3–4, 1781, Capt. John “Jack” Jouett spotted Banastre Tarleton’s British cavalry near Cuckoo Tavern in Virginia and rode roughly forty miles over back roads to warn Thomas Jefferson at Monticello and the Virginia Assembly at Charlottesville. Most of the government escaped; Virginia rewarded him with a sword and pistols. By 1782 he had moved west into what became Kentucky, represented Lincoln/Mercer and later Woodford counties as a statehood backer, and in 1797 built a brick Federal house on a 530-acre Woodford farm near Craig’s Creek — still standing as the Jack Jouett House Historic Site.

photo.title: Jack Jouett House Historic Site
photo.attribution: Day tripper · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

name: Shepherdsville / Salt River falls
subtitle: Adam Shepherd · Bullitt County seat · 1793
history: On December 11, 1793, the Kentucky General Assembly established a town on fifty acres of Adam Shepherd’s land on the north side of Salt River, at the falls where the great road to Bullitt’s Lick crossed. When Bullitt County was organized in 1796–97, Shepherdsville became the seat, anchoring settlement between the Wilderness Road corridor and the Falls of the Ohio salt trade.

name: Capt. Nathaniel Hart / White Oak Springs
subtitle: Hart’s Station · Madison County · 1779–1782
history: Capt. Nathaniel Hart (1734–1782), a Transylvania Company proprietor and chief negotiator with the Cherokee, came to Boonesborough in 1775 and in 1779 settled White Oak Springs (Hart’s Station) about a mile from the fort, joined by Dutch families from Pennsylvania. He was killed nearby in 1782; his daughter Susannah later married Isaac Shelby, Kentucky’s first and fifth governor.

name: Henderson / Red Banks
subtitle: Hopkins–Allin plan · April 6, 1797
history: The Ohio River bluff known as Red Banks sat on the Virginia grant later confirmed to Richard Henderson & Company. On April 6, 1797, Gen. Samuel Hopkins and surveyor Thomas Allin finished laying out the town of Henderson—named for the company founder, who had died in 1785. That plan is still treated as the city’s birthday; Henderson County followed in 1798–99.

name: Turk Site (15Ce6)
subtitle: Carlisle County · Mississippian Dorena–Medley
history: On a bluff spur near Bardwell overlooking the Mississippi floodplain, the Turk Site (15Ce6) was a small Mississippian regional center of about 2.5 hectares. Occupied mainly in the Dorena phase (about 1100–1300 CE) and into the Medley phase, it arranged platform mounds around a plaza—tightened by the spur’s narrow geography.

name: Lost River Cave
subtitle: Bowling Green · Pennyroyal karst · late-1700s mill
history: Under Bowling Green, Lost River Cave is a Pennyroyal karst system cut in Mississippian St. Louis and Ste. Genevieve limestones: a surface stream sinks into roughly seven miles of passages. Settlers harnessed the flow for a grist mill at the cave mouth by the late 1700s; today the preserve offers Kentucky’s only underground boat tour.

name: Hansen Site (15GP14)
subtitle: Greenup County · Scioto mouth terrace
history: Near South Portsmouth in Greenup County, the Hansen Site sits on an Ohio River terrace just upstream from Lower Shawneetown and across from the Scioto mouth. Excavations document Late Archaic summer camps around 2000 BCE, then denser Middle–Late Woodland communities (about 300–600 CE); Fort Ancient people used the terrace later.

name: Natural Bridge
subtitle: Corbin Sandstone arch · Powell–Wolfe · state park 1926
history: In Powell and Wolfe counties, a 78-foot-long, 65-foot-high arch of Corbin Sandstone (Breathitt Formation, Middle Pennsylvanian) spans a gorge on the Middle Fork of the Red River. Long a landmark for Indigenous hunters and settlers, the site became a railroad excursion stop in the 1890s and one of Kentucky’s original state parks in 1926.

name: David Snowden homeplace
subtitle: Lee County · St. Helens · Middle Fork Kentucky River
history: Historic Snowden homeplace near St. Helens (Lee County), on a knob by the Middle Fork Kentucky River (KY 52 east of Beattyville). David Snowden Sr. (1759 near Perth Amboy, N.J. – 1839 Estill Co.) served as a Revolutionary War frontier “Indian spy” and guard from Washington Co., Pa. (federal pension W9308), and also on Gen. Lachlan McIntosh’s 1778 Ohio campaign and Col. William Crawford’s 1782 Sandusky expedition; he married Nancy Hazelrigg in 1782. His son David Snowden Jr. (1786–1852) built a log cabin, kitchen, and quarters here about 1825; a later two-story clapboard house on sandstone had a wing that served as the St. Helens post office. The family also appears in Owsley County around 1850 before Lee County split. The abandoned house was photographed extensively and was reportedly demolished after a fire. Photos: https://abandonedonline.net/location/david-snowden-house/ and https://abandonedonline.net/david-snowden-jrs-house/ . Pension abstract: https://kygenweb.net/estill/military/revwar/snowden01.htm.

name: Ann McGinty
subtitle: First spinning wheel over Cumberland Gap · Harrodstown · d. 1815
history: Anne Kennedy (later Poage, Lindsay, and McGinty) crossed into Kentucky in September 1775 with a spinning wheel—the first brought over Cumberland Gap—and soon helped her husband William Poage build looms at Harrodstown. Their linsey-woolsey cloth became a frontier staple; she later ran an ordinary (tavern-inn) and is buried in the Fort Harrod Pioneer Cemetery (d. 1815).

name: Henry McKenna
subtitle: Fairfield · Nelson County · Old Line sour mash 1855–1883
history: Irish immigrant Henry McKenna of County Derry settled at Fairfield in Nelson County, began distilling in a mill shed by 1855 (under a barrel a day), and built a brick distillery by 1883. He sold only "H. McKenna Old Line" sour mash—never green whisky under three years—and stamped barrels with an Irish harp. The brand later survived Prohibition as medicinal whisky; Heaven Hill revived it in the modern era.

name: Estill Springs
subtitle: Estill County · Irvine · KY 89 (marker 555)
history: Mineral springs about half a mile north of Irvine on today’s KY 89, long known to Shawnee camps and early Kentucky explorers (Boone, Boyle, McAfee, and others). Operated as a resort from 1814 until the hotel burned in 1924; white sulphur water, Sweet Lick Knob views, and a popular ballroom drew visitors from across the state. In 1861 owner Col. Sidney M. Barnes organized the 8th Kentucky Infantry (USA) here; the grounds later hosted Confederate reunions of Morgan’s men, including the last. Kentucky Historical Society marker #555 stands on Main Street across from Estill Springs Elementary. Historic photo (c. 1910): https://scholarworks.moreheadstate.edu/sprague_photo_collection/117/

subtitle: Estill County · Irvine · c. 1908 (town-center pin)
history: The M. Robison Sawmill at Irvine, Estill County, Kentucky, circa 1908 — captured in the Stuart S. Sprague photograph collection. Map pin uses Irvine town center (Nominatim) because the exact mill footprint is not documented in the catalog record; treat as a place-level pin for the historic sawmill operation, not a surveyed building outline. name: John Finley
subtitle: Eskippakithiki trade ~1752 · Boone expedition guide 1769 · Clark County
history: Long before Wilderness Road fame, Pennsylvania-born trader John Finley (also Findley) was crossing the Alleghenies for furs. Around 1752 he reached Eskippakithiki, the Shawnee town in today’s Clark County, one of the earliest recorded Euro-American trading trips into central Kentucky. Years later, as a Braddock-campaign acquaintance of Daniel Boone, he returned to the Yadkin with stories of cane-rich hunting grounds beyond Cumberland Gap. In May 1769 he guided Boone’s party through that gap; Finley’s firsthand routes—not Boone alone—helped open the country settlers would soon claim.

name: Springfield / Washington County seat
subtitle: First county after statehood 1792 · town laid out 1793 · Matthew Walton
history: Washington County was the first county the new Kentucky legislature created after 1792 statehood, named for George Washington. In 1793 a site near the old Wilderness Trace was chosen for the seat on land tied to Gen. Matthew Walton; surveyor David Caldwell laid out the public square, and the town took the name Springfield. Early stations—Sandusky (1776), Cartwright’s (1778)—and Parker’s Landing on Beech Fork had already drawn settlers from the Gap road; Maryland Catholics arrived in force from 1785. The Lincoln family later settled nearby on Beech Fork, and Thomas Lincoln and Nancy Hanks’s marriage bond still sits in the Washington County clerk’s office.

name: Ruddell's Station
subtitle: Harrison County · fort 1779 · Bird capture June 1780 · South Fork Licking
history: In spring 1779 Capt. Isaac Ruddell rebuilt a fort on the South Fork of Licking (Harrison County) on the old Hinkson site—Ruddell’s Station, or Fort Liberty—soon joined by many Pennsylvania German families. In June 1780 British Capt. Henry Bird marched south with cannon, Canadian volunteers, and hundreds of Native allies. Artillery cracked the log walls; Ruddell surrendered under a promise of protection, then watched the agreement collapse as roughly four hundred captives were marched toward Detroit. Two of his sons were adopted by Shawnee; Stephen later lived as Tecumseh’s companion. The British never again brought that scale of artillery into Kentucky.

name: Simpsonville
subtitle: Shelby County · laid out 1816 · Capt. John Simpson namesake
history: In Shelby County, Isaac Watkins petitioned to lay out Simpsonville in 1816 as a waystation on the Louisville–Shelbyville road. A post office opened in 1821; the town incorporated in 1833. It was named for Capt. John Simpson, a Shelby County lawyer and Speaker of the Kentucky House (1810–11) who fought at Fallen Timbers (1794), won a seat in Congress in 1812, then died at the River Raisin on January 22, 1813. By the mid-1820s the place was a busy Midland Trail stage stop — home ground for anyone driving US 60 past Bagdad today.

photo.title: Bank of Simpsonville Building (1902)

name: Tolu Site (15Cn1)
subtitle: Crittenden County · Mississippian · occupation ~1200–1300 CE
history: Near Tolu in Crittenden County, the Tolu Site (15Cn1) was a Mississippian town occupied mainly about 1200–1300 CE (pottery styles; occupation into the 1400s). It once held three mounds — a platform, a burial mound, and a third of unclear use — and belongs to the Angel phase “Kincaid Set” with Angel (IN), Kincaid (IL), and Wickliffe (KY). Webb and Funkhouser excavated it in 1930; a 1954 plow find west of town produced one of the finest Mississippian fluorite statues known, complete with a rare beaded forelock.

name: Saltpeter Cave (Carter Caves)
subtitle: Carter County · War of 1812 niter mining · 15Cr99
history: In Carter County’s Carter Caves State Resort Park, Saltpeter Cave (15Cr99) was mined for potassium nitrate during the War of 1812, when British blockades forced Americans to scrape gunpowder ingredients from their own caves. University of Kentucky archaeologists in the early 1990s documented impressions and remnants of 26 wooden leaching vats — a hybrid of big-box and small V-shaped cottage setups with wooden piping. Kentucky caves yielded more than 300,000 pounds of saltpeter statewide; this one is on the National Register and open for summer tours.

photo.title: Saltpeter Cave, Carter Caves State Resort Park

name: Jenny Wiley / Big Sandy
subtitle: Captivity & escape 1789–1790 · Johnson Co. settlement 1800
history: On October 1, 1789, at Walker's Creek in present-day Bland County, Virginia, a Cherokee–Shawnee party seeking revenge on Matthias Harman mistakenly hit Thomas Wiley's cabin. Jenny (Virginia Sellards) Wiley saw her brother and three children killed; she and an infant were taken captive. Over nearly eleven months in the Big Sandy country the infant died and another child born in captivity was killed. She escaped by following a dream-path of creeks to Harman's Station near present-day Paintsville, where men built a log raft and pulled her across. Reunited with Thomas in Virginia, the couple settled on Tom's Creek in what became Johnson County in 1800; she died there in 1831. Jenny Wiley State Resort Park on Dewey Lake near Prestonsburg carries her name.

name: Buckner Site (15Bb12)
subtitle: Bourbon County · Fort Ancient occupation ~1200–1550 CE
history: Near Paris in Bourbon County, the Buckner Site (15Bb12) holds two circular Fort Ancient villages around central plazas, occupied mainly about A.D. 1200–1400 and into the early 1500s. Wall-trench houses, shell- and limestone-tempered pottery, triangular points, and a stone-paved McCray Mound mortuary area show maize farmers tied into Ohio Valley exchange. University of Kentucky WPA crews dug there in 1939; later work mapped the rings. It was listed on the National Register in 1983 (address restricted) — Bluegrass country that was already a settled farming landscape centuries before Paris or Bourbon whiskey.
geocode_note: NRHP address restricted; pinned to nearest city Paris, KY (Strodes Creek / Bourbon County).

name: McGary's Station / Shawnee Springs
subtitle: Mercer County · station ~1779 · McGary at Blue Licks 1782
history: Irish-born Hugh McGary (1744–1806) came into Kentucky in 1775 with Boone's party, settled near Fort Harrod, and built McGary's Station around 1779 at Shawnee Springs in today's Mercer County. On August 19, 1782, as a major under Col. John Todd, he commanded the center at Blue Licks. When Boone warned of an ambush at the Licking Ford, McGary rode across shouting for anyone who wasn't a coward to follow. The militia plunged into the trap; roughly seventy Kentuckians fell in minutes, including Todd and Israel Boone. McGary survived—and later killed the surrendered Shawnee chief Moluntha on Logan's 1786 Ohio raid, earning a court-martial suspension.

name: Bagdad / Consolation rail stop
subtitle: Shelby County · L&F Railroad ~1850 · post office 1861
history: Northeastern Shelby County's Bagdad grew because the Louisville and Frankfort Railroad reached the area about 1850. Earlier settlers clustered at Consolation, roughly a mile east, with a post office from 1849; once the depot and mill sat on the line, people drifted west and Consolation faded. On October 12, 1861, the Christiansburg post office moved to the station and took the name Bagdad, with Richard Radford as first postmaster. The place became a shipping point for flour, meal, livestock, and tobacco. Bagdad still sits at KY 12 and 395, about eleven miles northeast of Shelbyville.

name: Holder's Station / Lower Howard's Creek
subtitle: Clark County · station ~1782 · KY River flatboat hub
history: John Holder (1753–1799) came to Kentucky in 1777, fought under George Rogers Clark, and commanded Fort Boonesborough in 1779. In 1782 he planted Holder's Station about a mile downstream from Boonesborough on the north bank of the Kentucky River, near the mouth of Lower Howard's Creek in what became Clark County. The stockade grew into a store, tavern, ferry, warehouse, mill, and boatyard—a Kentucky River flatboat hub for New Orleans-bound produce and one of the Bluegrass's earliest industrial corridors. He married Fanny Callaway (one of the girls captured with Jemima Boone in 1776), sat as a Clark County justice under Governor Isaac Shelby, and is remembered on Kentucky Historical Marker 1048 and the John Holder Trail at Lower Howard's Creek Nature & Heritage Preserve.

name: Lebanon / Hardin's Creek Meeting House
subtitle: Marion County · meeting house 1789 · town 1814–15 · seat 1834
history: Lebanon grew around Hardin's Creek Meeting House, a Presbyterian congregation Virginia settlers planted in 1789. The town was formally established in 1814, incorporated in 1815, and named for the biblical Lebanon because of the cedar timber on nearby hills. It sat first in Nelson County, then Washington after 1792; when Marion County was cut from Washington in 1834, Lebanon became the seat—named for South Carolina's Revolutionary "Swamp Fox," Francis Marion. The early church nucleus still marks the center of Marion County's map.

photo.title: Marion County Courthouse, Lebanon

name: Sweet Lick Knob Fort Ancient public building
subtitle: Estill County · Fort Ancient public building ~1400–1450 CE
history: On the Kentucky River floodplain below Sweet Lick Knob near Irvine in Estill County, Fort Ancient people used a large rectangular public building from about 1400 to 1450 CE. University of Kentucky excavations documented a structure about 42 by 28 feet (roughly 1,176 square feet) with three deep sacred-pole pits and two rectangular hearths down the center—likely a place for periodic social or ritual meetings. Floor finds include every stage of sandstone disk production and ornaments of eastern Kentucky cannel coal. The site sits where mountain rockshelters to the east meet lowland villages to the west; the knob itself may have served as a landmark drawing dispersed Fort Ancient groups together. (Distinct from the Estill Springs resort pin, which notes Sweet Lick Knob views.)

name: Falmouth at the Licking Forks
subtitle: Pendleton County · town 1793 · county seat from 1799
history: Falmouth was established in 1793 at the confluence of the Main Licking and South Licking in what became Pendleton County. Virginians who settled there named it for Falmouth in Stafford County, Virginia. Pendleton County was formed in 1798 from parts of Bracken and Campbell (organized 1799) and named for Virginia statesman Edmund Pendleton; Falmouth has been the county seat ever since. The forks made the spot a natural river landing—Colonel Henry Bird's 1780 British–Indian expedition passed this way toward Ruddell's and Martin's Stations—and the town still sits where those two Licking branches meet, about thirty-nine miles south of Cincinnati.

photo.title: Pendleton County Courthouse, Falmouth

name: Worthington's Fort (Edward Worthington)
subtitle: Boyle County · fort ~1779 · 4 mi SE of Danville
history: Irish-born Edward Worthington (c. 1754–1804) reached the Kentucky country as a surveyor on Beargrass Creek by 1775, fought in Lord Dunmore's War, and was wounded defending McClelland's Station against Mingo warriors under Pluggy on December 29, 1776. As a captain and paymaster under George Rogers Clark he helped take Vincennes (1779), then planted Worthington's Fort about four miles southeast of present Danville. In 1780 Clark ordered his company to build Fort Jefferson on the Chickasaw Bluffs near the Ohio–Mississippi confluence; continuous Chickasaw pressure forced its abandonment in 1781. Worthington later died of yellow fever in New Orleans while chasing a land-fraud suit.
geocode_note: Approximate: Wikipedia places Worthington's Fort about four miles southeast of Danville; computed 6.4 km SE of Danville center. Exact stockade site not published.

name: Fort Jefferson (Clark's post on the Mississippi)
subtitle: Ballard County · Virginia post 1780–1781 · Worthington's company
history: In 1780 George Rogers Clark ordered Capt. Edward Worthington's company of the Illinois Regiment to occupy the bluffs just below the Ohio–Mississippi confluence and build Fort Jefferson, anchoring Virginia's claim to the Mississippi and guarding Illinois County against river-borne threats from the south. Settler families joined a small civil town (Clarksville) beside the post, but the fort sat on Chickasaw land without their consent; continuous Chickasaw pressure, sickness, and short supplies made it indefensible, and Worthington withdrew the garrison and abandoned it in 1781. Fort Jefferson Hill at Wickliffe, with its memorial cross above the confluence, marks the vicinity today (KHS marker 1309, Fort Jefferson Site).
geocode_note: Wikipedia Fort Jefferson (Kentucky) coordinates; KHS marker 1309 at 36.9556, -89.09115. Distinct from Wickliffe Mounds pin (~2 km north).

name: Paducah — 1827 William Clark plat
subtitle: McCracken County · platted 1827 · incorporated 1830 · seat 1832
history: After the 1818 Jackson Purchase opened Chickasaw land west of the Tennessee River, a small landing called Pekin grew at the Ohio–Tennessee confluence. In 1827 William Clark (of Lewis and Clark, then Superintendent of Indian Affairs) platted a town on that ground and named it Paducah for the Padouca, a people he had known on the plains and believed nearly erased by European expansion—not the later folk legend of a Chickasaw "Chief Paduke." The town incorporated in 1830 and became McCracken County's seat in 1832, riding steamboat traffic into a river-and-rail hub.

name: Slack Farm (15Un28) Caborn-Welborn village
subtitle: Union County · Caborn-Welborn village ~1400–1700 CE
history: On the Ohio River floodplain in Union County, Slack Farm was a large Caborn-Welborn Mississippian village occupied about 1400–1700 CE. Across roughly 75 acres, residents built at least seven residential clusters with wall-trench wattle-and-daub houses, deep corn-storage pits, and cemeteries oriented toward plazas. Long-distance trade reached north for catlinite and south for Nodena points and marine shell; by about 1550, glass beads and reworked brass show indirect European contact. After severe looting in 1987, Kentucky Heritage Council, University of Kentucky, and Indiana University crews—with hundreds of volunteers—mapped more than 450 looter holes and documented the village layout before reinterring remains on site.
geocode_note: Deliberately generalized to the Uniontown / Ohio floodplain vicinity; archaeological site coordinates are not published (site was looted in 1987).

name: Craig's Station / Travelling Church (Gilbert's Creek)
subtitle: Garrard County · Travelling Church arrives Dec 1781 · near Lancaster
history: In fall–winter 1781, Rev. Lewis Craig led roughly 200 Baptists and about 400 other settlers from Spotsylvania County, Virginia—the largest single pioneer party yet to enter the Kentucky District. Capt. William Ellis guided the train through Cumberland Gap; they raised a fortified meetinghouse and Craig's Station at Gilbert's Creek (near present Lancaster) that December. Members later founded Gilbert's Creek Baptist (still active), South Elkhorn, Clear Creek, and other congregations that seeded central Kentucky's Baptist landscape. Lewis's brother Elijah stayed behind in Virginia awhile to press for religious liberty with James Madison before following west.
geocode_note: Geotag of the Commons photo of the Colonial Dames 'Travelling Church, 1781' memorial below the hilltop church site on Gilbert's Creek, SE of Lancaster.

name: Hubbell's Flatboat Fight — Limestone Landing
subtitle: Mason County · Ohio River flatboat stand, March 23 1791 · landed at Limestone (Maysville)
history: On March 23, 1791, Capt. William Hubbell of the Frankfort frontier was taking a flatboat down the Ohio toward Limestone (today’s Maysville) with Daniel Light, William Plascut’s family, and others—about twenty souls after late pickups. At dawn near the Kanawha country, three Indian canoes closed in. Hubbell’s nine armed men held a running fight; he kept firing after a ball wrecked his gun lock, used a firebrand to touch off another shot, then drove boarders back with pistols and firewood even after a bullet tore his right arm. Two of his men died in the boat, another later at Limestone; the women and children survived. The party reached Limestone that night. A companion boat under Capt. Greathouse, which had not prepared to fight, was taken ashore with grim results.
geocode_note: Approximate Limestone landing on the Maysville riverfront near the mouth of Limestone Creek, where Hubbell's boat put in the night of the fight. The attack itself happened upriver on the Ohio; the pin marks the landing.

name: Augusta founding / Capt. Philip Buckner
subtitle: Bracken County · 600-acre town grant 1797 · early county seat
history: Captain Philip Buckner, a Revolutionary War commissary officer with Virginia land grants in what became Bracken County, gave 600 acres to lay out Augusta in 1797. The Kentucky legislature chartered the river town that October; Augusta served as Bracken’s early county seat. Buckner later sat in the 1799 constitutional convention and the legislature, and lived many years at Woodlawn before dying in 1830. Augusta’s Ohio-River landing put northeastern Kentucky on a main corridor between Limestone and Cincinnati long before Covington filled the Licking Point.
geocode_note: Augusta town center on the Ohio River. KHS marker #1502 (Founder of Augusta) stands at Powersville near Buckner's Woodlawn, not in town.

name: Egushawa's Odawa at Martin's Station
subtitle: Bourbon County · Odawa war chief with Bird's invasion · Martin's Station 1780 · Greenville 1795
history: Egushawa (also Au-goosh-away), the Detroit-area Odawa war chief often treated as Pontiac’s successor, helped Britain recruit Wabash and Great Lakes allies against Kentucky settlements. In 1780 he led an Ottawa contingent with Capt. Henry Bird’s cannon-backed invasion that forced the surrenders at Ruddell’s and Martin’s stations and marched hundreds of prisoners north toward Detroit. After 1783 he rejected land cessions made without tribal consent, fought in the Northwest Confederacy’s victories over Harmar and St. Clair, was wounded at Fallen Timbers in 1794, and signed Greenville in 1795 as a principal Ottawa spokesman—tying Odawa strategy on the Maumee and Detroit to the raids that shaped Kentucky’s last Revolutionary decade.
geocode_note: ExploreKYHistory location for KHS marker #150 (Martin's Station), ~3 mi NW of Paris on Stoner Creek — the second station Bird's force (including Egushawa's Ottawa band) took in June 1780. Distinct from the existing Ruddell's Station pin.

name: Cloudsplitter Rockshelter (15Mf36)
subtitle: Menifee County · Red River Gorge · Late Archaic squash & early plant tending
history: In the Red River Gorge sandstone country, Cloudsplitter Rockshelter holds a deep Archaic-to-Early Woodland record. Dry sand preserved a roughly 3,700-year-old squash rind—early evidence that people here were tending plants—as well as chipped and ground stone tools and pollen that tracks climate change. Later Woodland layers at Cloudsplitter and neighboring Gorge shelters (Newt Kash, Haystack, Rogers) show storage pits, seed crops such as sunflower, sumpweed, maygrass, and knotweed, and a shift from nut-heavy foraging toward small-scale gardens. The Gorge’s dry shelters are why eastern Kentucky figures so largely in the story of plant domestication in eastern North America.
geocode_note: Pinned at the named Cloud Splitter natural arch (TopoQuest / USGS Pomeroyton quad, Menifee Co.). Exact 15Mf36 rockshelter coordinates are not published (address-restricted archaeological site). Years are Late Archaic occupation (~4500–3000 BP / −3000…−1000), not the 1978 excavation.

name: Ephraim McDowell House — first ovariotomy (1809)
subtitle: Boyle County · Danville · Jane Todd Crawford surgery, Dec 25 1809
history: On Christmas Day 1809 in Danville, Dr. Ephraim McDowell—Scotch-Irish, Edinburgh-trained, practicing on the Kentucky frontier since 1795—removed a 22.5-pound ovarian tumor from Jane Todd Crawford of Greensburg. She had ridden roughly sixty miles believing she was overdue in pregnancy; McDowell diagnosed a cyst and operated in his home without anesthesia or antisepsis while assistants held her. The surgery lasted about twenty-five minutes. Crawford recovered and lived more than three decades more. McDowell’s later reports helped prove that opening the abdomen need not be a death sentence, making Danville a landmark in the history of surgery west of the Alleghenies.

name: Mary Ingles at Big Bone Lick (1755 escape)
subtitle: Boone County · Shawnee captive at the salt camp · escape ~mid-Oct 1755 · KHS marker
history: In July 1755 a Shawnee war party struck Draper's Meadow on the Virginia frontier and carried Mary Draper Ingles, then about twenty-three and pregnant, west with her two young sons. After the long march to the Ohio villages she was put to work at a salt-making camp at Big Bone Lick in what is now Boone County—among the earliest recorded European women on Kentucky ground. Around mid-October she slipped away with an older Dutch captive woman and walked the Ohio, Kanawha, and New River corridors for roughly forty-two days, foraging on walnuts, grapes, and roots until she reached a New River cabin near her old home. Her son Thomas was later ransomed; she lived until 1815. The Kentucky Historical Society marker at Big Bone Lick still marks the breakout that turned a captivity story into one of the frontier's great return journeys.
geocode_note: KHS marker #859 'Mary Ingles' at Big Bone Lick State Park (KY 338). Distinct from the existing Big Bone Lick fossil-lick pin (Pleistocene / Gist / Jefferson).

name: Bowling Green founding / Bolin Green (1798)
subtitle: Warren County seat · Robert & George Moore land · Fountain Square · town laid out 1798
history: Long hunters marked the Barren River country in 1775; McFadden's Station rose on the north bank in 1778. In the mid-1790s brothers Robert and George Moore settled by a big spring, and when Warren County was created they donated land for a log courthouse and jail—today's Fountain Square. On more than thirty additional acres the county court laid out a town in early 1798 and named it Bolin Green, recalling New York's Bowling Green where patriots had pulled down King George's statue. The settlement won the county seat in 1809 and incorporated in 1812, growing into south-central Kentucky's commercial hub on the river and later the Louisville & Nashville road.
geocode_note: Fountain Square Park, the Moore brothers' courthouse-square donation and center of the 1798 town plat.

name: E.H. Taylor Jr. / Old Taylor Distillery — Bottled-in-Bond Act (1897)
subtitle: Franklin County · Millville (Glenn's Creek) · Taylor's castle distillery · Bottled-in-Bond Act signed Mar 3 1897
history: Colonel Edmund Haynes Taylor Jr. (1830–1923) of Frankfort rebuilt Kentucky whiskey's reputation after the Civil War—raising the O.F.C. (Old Fire Copper) plant in 1869, later the Old Taylor works on Glenn's Creek, and fighting the flood of adulterated "rectified" spirits. Working with Treasury Secretary John G. Carlisle, he helped push the Bottled-in-Bond Act, signed March 3, 1897: one distiller, one distillery, one season; at least four years in wood under federal lock; bottled at 100 proof with nothing added but water. It was among the nation's first consumer-protection laws for spirits, and the green bond stamp became the buyer's guarantee that what was in the bottle was straight whiskey—not prune juice and industrial alcohol.
geocode_note: Old Taylor Distillery (now Castle & Key), 4445 McCracken Pike, Millville — E.H. Taylor Jr.'s Old Taylor plant, which he operated in 1897. His 1869 O.F.C. plant (now Buffalo Trace) was under George T. Stagg by then, so the Old Taylor works is the better-supported pin.

name: Singer-Hieronymus Site Complex (15Sc3 / 15Sc225)
subtitle: Scott County · North Elkhorn Creek ridge · circular Fort Ancient villages ~1200–1550
history: On a broad ridge overlooking North Elkhorn Creek in Scott County, just north of Lexington, Fort Ancient farmers built a chain of circular villages between about A.D. 1200 and 1550. UK archaeologists mapped Singer Village in the late 1990s, then found more rings on the adjoining Hieronymus farm; later geophysics pushed the count to at least six or seven midden stains—concentric house, burial, and trash zones around open plazas, with corn-beans-squash agriculture and two low burial mounds on the largest circle. The complex looks like one community shifting along the ridge over generations, a rare Kentucky window on how Fort Ancient towns moved without leaving the same bluegrass creek.
geocode_note: Generalized pin on North Elkhorn Creek in Scott County. Exact 15Sc3/15Sc225 coordinates are not published (address-restricted archaeological site). Years are Fort Ancient occupation (~A.D. 1200–1550), not the 1920s/1990s/2010s investigations.

name: Levi Todd / Ellerslie (Lexington co-founder)
subtitle: Fayette County · Levi Todd's Ellerslie on Richmond Road · Lexington trustee 1776, county clerk, Blue Licks major · Kentucky career 1775–1807
history: Levi Todd (1756–1807) came to Kentucky in 1775 with his brothers John and Robert, helped lay out Lexington’s stockade, and was elected one of its first Gentlemen Trustees in March 1776. He became Kentucky County’s first clerk in 1777, rode with George Rogers Clark’s Illinois campaign (including the capture of Kaskaskia in 1778), and later served decades as Fayette County clerk. In August 1782 he led a forty-man relief column toward Bryan Station, then fought at Blue Licks—where brother Col. John Todd was killed—and wrote one of the earliest official accounts of the defeat. He rose to major general of Kentucky militia, built Ellerslie (Fayette’s first brick house), and was grandfather of Mary Todd Lincoln.
geocode_note: KHS marker #1001 'Ellerslie', 2440 Richmond Rd., Lexington — site of the brick house Levi Todd built in 1787. Distinct from the existing Col. John Todd (his brother) pin in downtown Lexington. Years are Levi Todd's Kentucky career (arrived 1775, died 1807), not the house's later history.

name: New Castle — Henry County seat (1798)
subtitle: Henry County · county cut from Shelby 1798 · courthouse square · incorporated 1817
history: When the General Assembly cut Henry County from Shelby County in 1798 and named it for Virginia’s Patrick Henry, New Castle was fixed as the seat—just north of Shelby County, inside the Louisville–Lexington–Cincinnati triangle. Landowners opened a courthouse square; the town was incorporated in 1817 and is counted among Kentucky’s oldest incorporated communities. Tobacco, hay, and cattle long carried the surrounding farms, and the courthouse square still anchors a preserved downtown. The 1863 Caplinger House, built by druggist James N. Caplinger, was the Henry County History Center until it was sold in 2017 and became a private residence.
geocode_note: Town center / courthouse square, New Castle (Wikipedia coordinates 38.4333, -85.1689; KHS 'County Named, 1798' marker stands on the courthouse lawn). Year is the 1798 county and county-seat creation, not the 1875 courthouse or 1863 Caplinger House. name: Dover Mound (Adena burial mound, Mason County)
subtitle: Mason County · Ohio River hills near Dover · Adena burial mound · 55 burials reported
history: On a ridge near Dover in Mason County, the Dover Mound was an Adena (Early Woodland) burial mound. University of Kentucky anthropologists William S. Webb and Charles E. Snow excavated it in the early 1950s and reported fifty-five burials with accompanying artifacts—one of the fuller published Adena mortuary assemblages from northern Kentucky’s Ohio River hills. Their 1959 monograph still anchors what we know of the site and places Dover in the same Adena world as Mount Horeb and other Bluegrass earthworks, centuries before Fort Ancient villages lined the same river.
geocode_note: Generalized pin at Dover, Mason County. Exact mound coordinates are not published in the cited source (University Press of Kentucky page). Years are the Adena occupation span (~800 B.C.–A.D. 700 default), NOT the early-1950s Webb–Snow excavation or the 1959 monograph.

name: Bryan Station siege (Aug 15–16, 1782)
subtitle: Fayette County · Elkhorn Creek north of Lexington · women at the spring · Caldwell–Girty force
history: Bryan Station (also Bryan’s / Bryant’s) sat on the south bank of Elkhorn Creek a few miles northeast of Lexington, planted in 1776 by the Bryan brothers and Boone in-laws from North Carolina. On August 15–16, 1782, Capt. William Caldwell, Simon Girty, and several hundred British-allied Wyandot, Lenape, and Shawnee warriors surrounded the fort. Knowing the attackers hoped to ambush men at the spring, the garrison sent the women and girls out with their usual water pails; they filled the fort’s supply and returned unharmed. The siege failed to take the station; when Kentucky militia pursued three days later, they met disaster at Blue Licks.
geocode_note: Bryan Station site on the south bank of Elkhorn Creek (Wikipedia coordinates 38.0759, -84.4153), near the Bryan Station Memorial. No existing History-pack pin; the Blue Licks pin is the later, separate battle of Aug 19, 1782. KHS marker #21 (Bryan's Station) is in the markers layer.

name: James Knox / Camp Knox (Skinhouse Branch)
subtitle: Green County · Skinhouse Branch · long-hunter base camp ~1770 · Dix River tradition · KY Senate 1795–1800
history: Before Boone’s fame crowded the memory, Scots-Irish long hunter James Knox led parties through Cumberland Gap into Kentucky’s Green River country. Around 1770 his men built a “skin house” pelt camp on what is still called Skinhouse Branch in Green County—Camp Knox on the markers. Tradition holds that Cherokee hunter Captain Dick guided him and that Knox named Dix River for that guide. Knox later raised a company for Virginia’s 8th Regiment, fought with Morgan’s Rifles at Saratoga, and sat in the Kentucky Senate from Lincoln County (1795–1800).
geocode_note: HMDB Historic Camp Knox marker at Skinhouse Branch Rd (SR 2188) & Long Hunters Camp Rd (SR 767), Green County (37°10.22′N 85°22.929′W). Distinct from Fort Knox (Hardin County). Years are the ~1770 camp through Knox’s Kentucky Senate service (to 1800).

name: Somerset — Pulaski County seat (1801)
subtitle: Pulaski County · William Dodson donation · Town Spring · named for Somerset County, N.J.
history: Pulaski County needed a seat after its 1799 creation from Lincoln and Green. In 1801 the court laid out Somerset on forty acres donated by William Dodson, beside a dependable spring whose path became the town’s busiest early street. Migrants from Somerset County, New Jersey, gave the place its name. Kentucky Historical Society Marker 1607 still marks the Old Town Spring—where locals joked that whoever drank would gain wisdom and always return.
geocode_note: Town center, Somerset (Wikipedia 37.0844, -84.6081). Year is the 1801 court layout / county seat, not the 1799 county creation. KHS Marker 1607 (Old Town Spring) is in the markers layer.

name: Mammoth Cave saltpeter (War of 1812)
subtitle: Edmonson County · Historic Entrance / Rotunda · industrial nitrate mining 1812–1815 · enslaved labor
history: Long before tourism, Mammoth Cave’s nitrate-rich dirt fed gunpowder. In the War of 1812, when British blockade cut imported saltpeter, operators worked the Rotunda and nearby passages at industrial scale—leaching cave soil in wooden vats, pumping liquor to the surface, and converting it to potassium nitrate. Enslaved laborers did most of the hauling and filtering; remnants of vats, pipes, and pump works still stand just inside the Historic Entrance. After 1815 cheap imports killed the market, and the same passages became Kentucky’s first great show cave.
geocode_note: Mammoth Cave Historic Entrance (OSM/Nominatim). Distinct from Salts Cave (15Ht4) Early Woodland sulfate mining, Great Saltpetre Cave (Rockcastle), and Saltpeter Cave at Carter Caves. Years are War of 1812 industrial production (1812–1815), not park establishment.
